theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Array Addressing and String Internals

The row-major formula follows from counting. For an array with M rows and N columns, reaching m[i][j] means skipping i complete rows of N elements each and then j more elements in row i, so the element sits i × N + j places after the first one; multiplying by the element size w gives the byte offset. Column-major order, used by Fortran and MATLAB, stores whole columns one after another, so the count becomes j × M + i. Languages whose indices may start at another lower bound, such as Pascal's A[1..10], subtract the bounds first, while C indices always start at 0. Because the compiler needs N to evaluate the formula, every dimension except the first must appear in a parameter declaration.

theoryAdd.plainText: Row-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((i - Lr) * N + (j - Lc)), where N = number of columns and Lr, Lc = lower bounds (0 in C)
Column-major: Loc(A[i][j]) = B + w * ((j - Lc) * M + (i - Lr)), where M = number of rows

theoryAdd.text: Details of the <string.h> functions that questions like to test:
items: strncpy(d, s, n) copies at most n characters; if s is shorter it pads d with '\0' up to n, and if s has n or more characters it writes no terminator at all.
strcat(d, s) starts writing at the '\0' of d, so d must already hold a terminated string and have room for strlen(d) + strlen(s) + 1 bytes.
strcmp compares characters as unsigned char values and stops at the first difference or at the end; the standard guarantees only the sign of the result, not a value such as 1 or -1.
strchr(s, c) and strrchr(s, c) return a pointer into s (subtract s to get the index) or NULL; the terminating '\0' counts as part of the string, so strchr(s, '\0') points at the end.
strstr(s, t) returns a pointer to the first occurrence of t or NULL, and an empty t matches at once, so strstr(s, "") returns s.
strlen walks the whole string on every call, so for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++) can cost O(n²) steps; store the length in a variable first.
fgets keeps the newline the user typed, while scanf("%s") stops at the first space or newline and leaves the rest in the input buffer.

theoryAdd.text: Before an address calculation, settle four things: row-major or column-major order, the lower bounds (always 0 in C), the element size in bytes, and whether the given base is the address of the first element. The answer is then base + (number of elements skipped) × (element size).

questions.explanation: A partial initialiser fills a[0..2] with 3, 1, 4 and sets every remaining element to 0, so a[4] = 0. Then a[5] = 3 + 1 = 4.

questions.questionText: Which of the following declarations is INVALID in C?
questions.explanation: Only the first dimension may be left for the compiler to count from the initialiser; the column size must be given because it fixes the length of every row. int a[][2] is therefore valid while int a[2][] is not.
sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) is the element count, 6, whatever the size of int. a[6 / 2] = a[3] is the fourth element, 20.

questions.questionText: A global array int g[4]; is declared outside all functions without an initialiser. What are its elements at program start?
options: g[0] is 0 and the rest are garbage
questions.explanation: Global and static arrays have static storage duration and are zero-initialised before main runs. Only automatic (local) arrays without an initialiser hold indeterminate values.

questions.questionText: Given the declarations int a[3] = {1, 2, 3}, b[3]; which statement is correct?
options: b = a; is a compile error, because an array name cannot be assigned
b = a; copies all three elements of a into b
a == b compares the two arrays element by element
b[3] = a[2]; stores 3 in the last element of b
questions.explanation: An array name is not a modifiable lvalue, so arrays are copied with a loop or memcpy. a == b compares two addresses, and the last element of b is b[2], so b[3] is out of bounds.
Copying in place overwrites values before they are read: a[0] = a[4] = 5, a[1] = a[3] = 4, a[2] = 3, then a[3] = a[1] (now 4) and a[4] = a[0] (now 5). A real reversal swaps pairs up to the middle.

questions.questionText: What happens when a C program executes a[10] = 5; for an array declared int a[10]; ?
options: The compiler always rejects the statement
The array automatically grows to 11 elements
An array-index-out-of-bounds exception is raised at run time
Nothing checks the index: the write goes outside the array and the behaviour is undefined
questions.explanation: The valid indices are 0 to 9 and C performs no bounds checking, so a[10] writes into whatever memory follows the array. The result is undefined behaviour, which may corrupt other variables or crash.

Each inner brace initialises one row and zero-fills the rest of it: rows are {1, 0, 0}, {2, 3, 0}, {4, 5, 6}. So m[0][1] = 0, m[1][1] = 3 and s = 1 + 0 = 1; 2 5 7 would be the result without the inner braces.
The loop adds the main diagonal 1 + 5 + 9 = 15 and the other diagonal 3 + 5 + 7 = 15. The centre element 5 lies on both and is added twice, so s = 30.
Row 1 of A times column 1 of B: 4 * 0 + 5 * 1 + 6 * 2 = 17, which is C[1][1]. C[0][1] would be 8 and C[1][0] would be 16.
sizeof works in bytes: the whole array is 3 * 5 * 4 = 60, one row m[0] is an array of 5 ints = 20 (it is not converted to a pointer inside sizeof), and one element is 4.

questions.questionText: The array int a[20] starts at address 3000 and an int occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of a[12]?
questions.explanation: &a[i] = base + i * size = 3000 + 12 * 4 = 3048. Using 11 (counting from 1) would give 3044, and forgetting the element size gives 3012.

questions.questionText: The array double m[5][6] is stored in C's row-major order starting at address 1200, and a double occupies 8 bytes. What is the address of m[3][4]?
questions.explanation: Address = base + (i * cols + j) * size = 1200 + (3 * 6 + 4) * 8 = 1200 + 176 = 1376. Column-major order would give 1200 + (4 * 5 + 3) * 8 = 1384.

questions.questionText: A two-dimensional array A[1..10][1..15] (rows 1 to 10, columns 1 to 15) of 2-byte elements is stored row by row, and A[1][1] is at address 500. What is the address of A[6][8]?
questions.explanation: Subtract the lower bounds first: 500 + ((6 - 1) * 15 + (8 - 1)) * 2 = 500 + 82 * 2 = 664. Column-major order would give 500 + (7 * 10 + 5) * 2 = 650, and ignoring the lower bounds gives 696.

questions.questionText: The array int x[4][5] starts at address 1000 and an int occupies 4 bytes. Which element is stored at address 1068?
questions.explanation: The offset is (1068 - 1000) / 4 = 17 elements. In row-major order 17 = i * 5 + j gives i = 3 and j = 2; x[1][4] would be the column-major reading (17 = 4 * 4 + 1).

questions.questionText: The array int c[2][3][4] starts at address 4000 and an int occupies 4 bytes. What is the address of c[1][2][3]?
questions.explanation: Offset = ((i * d2 + j) * d3 + k) * size = ((1 * 3 + 2) * 4 + 3) * 4 = 23 * 4 = 92 bytes, so the address is 4000 + 92 = 4092.
The array parameter receives the address of x[0], so the additions change x itself: x becomes 10, 21, 32, 43. n is an ordinary int passed by value, so main's n stays 4.

The five values fill the array row by row, three per row, so the compiler makes 2 rows: a[0] = {1, 2, 3} and a[1] = {4, 5, 0}. sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) divides the whole array by the size of one row, giving 2, and a[1][2] is the element left without a value, which is set to 0.
The function returns an index, not a value. Because the test is >=, the later 9 at index 3 replaces the earlier one at index 1; with > the answer would be 1.
m[1] is the second row, an array of 3 ints that decays to &m[1][0], so sum adds 4 + 5 + 6 = 15.
const int a[] means the function may read the elements but not assign to them, so a[1] = t is rejected. n is an ordinary copy and may be changed freely.
The array holds A, B, '\0', C, D plus the terminating '\0' the compiler adds, so sizeof is 6. strlen stops at the first '\0', after 2 characters.

questions.questionText: In C, which statement about the declaration char a[3] = "ABC"; is correct?
options: It is a compile error in C, because the string needs 4 bytes
The compiler silently enlarges a to 4 elements
a holds 'A', 'B' and '\0'; the 'C' is dropped
It is valid C, but a holds no '\0', so passing a to strlen or printf("%s") is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: C allows the terminating null to be dropped when the array has exactly as many elements as the literal has characters, so a holds A, B, C only. It is then not a string, and functions that search for '\0' read past the end; C++ rejects this declaration.
a is an array of 7 chars (6 letters + '\0'), so sizeof(a) = 7, but p is a pointer, so sizeof(p) = 8 regardless of the text. strlen counts 6 characters in both cases.
sizeof gives the declared size, 12, whatever the contents. After s[2] = '\0' the string s is "he", so strlen(s) = 2, while s + 3 starts at the 'l' after the new terminator and prints lo.

questions.questionText: Given char a[] = "hi"; and char *p = "hi"; which statement is correct?
options: Both a[0] = 'H' and p[0] = 'H' are allowed
a[0] = 'H' is allowed, but p[0] = 'H' is undefined behaviour because p points to a string literal
Neither is allowed, because both are string constants
p[0] = 'H' is allowed, but a[0] = 'H' is a compile error
questions.explanation: a is a writable array initialised with a copy of the text, whereas p holds the address of the literal itself, which the program must not modify (it is often in read-only memory). Declaring const char *p makes the compiler catch such writes.
An array name cannot appear on the left of =, so a = "exam"; is rejected; the text must be copied with strcpy. A pointer can be pointed at a literal or at the array at any time.
n1 is an array of 3 pointers, 3 * 8 = 24 bytes (the literals live elsewhere). n2 reserves 3 rows of 7 chars, 21 bytes, even though "C" needs only 2 of its 7.

questions.questionText: Which <string.h> function appends a copy of one string to the end of another?
questions.explanation: strcat(d, s) writes s starting at the terminating '\0' of d. strcpy overwrites d from the start, strcmp compares and strstr searches for a substring.
strcat adds no space: a becomes CodeBlocks, 4 + 6 = 10 characters. sizeof(a) is still the declared 20 bytes.
Equal strings give 0, so x = 1. 'Z' (90) is less than 'a' (97), so "Zoo" sorts before "apple" and y = 1. "abc" differs from "ab" where 'c' meets '\0', and 'c' is larger, so z = 1.

questions.questionText: Assuming the ASCII character set, which of the following does the C standard guarantee about the value returned by strcmp("cat", "car")?
questions.explanation: The strings first differ at index 2, where 't' (116) is greater than 'r' (114), so the result is positive. The standard fixes only the sign; the actual value (1, 2 or anything else) is up to the library.

strncpy copies at most n = 2 characters and adds no '\0' when the source is longer than n, so only d[0] and d[1] change. The original terminator at d[7] is still there, and the string printed is EX followed by five stars.

questions.questionText: The array char d[5]; has been declared. Which call writes past the end of d?
questions.explanation: strcpy always copies the terminator, so "hello" needs 6 bytes and overflows d. "hell" needs exactly 5; strncpy with n = 5 writes exactly 5 bytes (for "hello" without any '\0', for "hi" padded with '\0').
strchr returns a pointer to the first 'g' and strrchr to the last one; subtracting s turns each pointer into a 0-based index. In p-r-o-g-r-a-m-m-i-n-g they are at indices 3 and 10.
strstr returns a pointer to the first match, and printing it with %s shows the rest of the string from there. "ab" first occurs at index 3 (abase) and "ba" at index 4 (base).
After each match p moves on by only one character, so overlapping matches are counted: "aba" is found at indices 0, 2 and 4, giving 3. Advancing by strlen("aba") = 3 instead would count 2.
Each character is copied and then tested, so the '\0' is copied as well before the loop stops. i is incremented only for the 4 letters, leaving i = 4, and dst holds LOOP.

strchr returns a non-NULL pointer exactly when s[i] is one of the listed vowels. Engineering has E, i, e, e, i (5) and Council has o, u, i (3), so v = 8; the capital E counts because uppercase vowels are in the list.
Every letter has its case toggled: P becomes p, r and o become R and O, and C becomes c. toupper leaves the space unchanged, giving pRO c.

The loop runs over the whole string instead of stopping at n / 2, so every pair is swapped twice: for i = 0 and i = 4 the pair (0, 4) is exchanged and then exchanged back. The string ends unchanged; the condition should be i < n / 2.
The %s conversion skips leading white space and stops reading at the next white-space character, so only Kathmandu is stored; Valley stays in the input buffer. fgets would read the whole line.
fgets stores the newline typed by the user, so buf holds 'H', 'i', '\n', '\0' and strlen(buf) = 3. The usual fix is buf[strcspn(buf, "\n")] = '\0'.
